Learning Objectives
Review the Seddon/Sunderland nerve classification and how the increasing degree of injury
affects the likelihood of recovery and the need for surgical management.
Explain how to appropriately grade muscle strength on physical examination and how to
localize peripheral nerve injury on motor examination.
Review the basic principles of electromyography, particularly the concept of fibrillations and
their association with the degree of nerve injury.
Explain the American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale for a spinal cord injury and
what spinal shock indicates.
Discuss the two mechanisms by which the spinal cord is injured (eg, mechanical and
physiologic) and potential targets for decreasing secondary injury.

Peripheral Nerve Injury

Peripheral Nerve Injury
All orthopaedic surgeons encounter peripheral nerve injuries in their practice. These
injuries can create a substantial amount of anxiety for the patient and the surgeon. This
is especially true if concern for an iatrogenic injury exists. To better understand the
management of peripheral nerve injuries, orthopaedic surgeon must understand
peripheral nerve injuries.
Means of Injury
A peripheral nerve injury can occur via various mechanisms, including the following:
Transection
Crush
Traction without rupture
Traction with rupture
Ischemic
Autoimmune
Response to Injury
Initial inflammatory response
Increased epineurial permeability and edema because no blood-nerve barrier for vessels is
present in the epineurium.
With disruption of the endoneurium (eg, transection), the blood-nerve barrier is disrupted,
increasing the permeability of endoneurial capillaries.
Ischemia and compression

Increased endoneurial pressure, fluid edema, and capillary permeability without affecting the
perineurial vascular system
Positive fluid pressure inside the endoneurium affects blood flow, decreasing nutrition and
oxygen delivery.
Persistent intraneural edema may diminish nerve function.
Classification of Peripheral Nerve Injuries
Seddon Classification
Neurapraxia
Immediate, localized blocking of neural conduction with normal conduction above the level
of injury
Typically reversible; axon continuity is maintained, but local demyelination and ischemia
occur.
Mechanisms of injury: compression, traction, contusion
Axonotmesis
Axon disruption without the destruction of Schwann cells, the perineurium, or the
epineurium; Wallerian degeneration occurs; axon distal to the injury degenerates.
Some nerve function may recover because the intact neural connective tissue layer (eg, intact
endoneurium) guides neural regeneration.
Mechanisms of injury: crush and forceful stretching
Neurotmesis
Complete disruption of the nerve
No recovery of function
Mechanisms of injury: open crush, violent stretch, and laceration
Sunderland Classification
The Sunderland nerve classification revised the Seddon classification into types (1 through 5),
with axonotmesis divided into three types (2 through 4) based on the degree of disruption of
nerve contents1 (Table 1).
Type 1: neurapraxia
Type 2: axonotmesis; axonal disruption with intact endoneurium, perineurium, and
epineurium.

Type 3: axonotmesis; axonal and endoneurium disrupted with intact perineurium and
epineurium.
Type 4: axonotmesis/neuroma in continuity; axonal, endoneurium, perineurium disrupted
with intact epineurium.
Type 5: neurotmesis
Mackinnon Modification
Type 6 was added, which is a mixed injury (combination of types 1 through 5).

The two nerve ends often retract as Wallerian degeneration is initiated by granular
disintegration of the axonal cytoskeleton.
At the proximal end of the injury, the cell body (nucleus) of the neuron swells and is displaced
peripherally. Chromatolysis (dispersion of basophilic Nissl granules with relative eosinophilia
of cell body) ensues.
Nerve cell stops producing neurotransmitters and begins synthesizing proteins required for
neural regeneration.
During Wallerian degeneration, Schwann cells and hematogenously derived macrophages
become active in clearing myelin and axonal debris from the site of injury.
Compression: Acute and Chronic
Nerve fibers are deformed, local ischemia occurs, vascular permeability increases.
Edema negatively affects the endoneurial environment, impairing axonal transport and nerve
dysfunction.
Eventually, fibroblasts invade the nerve-producing scar tissue, impairing gliding of nerve
fascicles over one another.
Tissue pressures of 30 mm Hg may cause paresthesia. Pressure greater than 60 mm Hg can
completely block nerve conduction.
Chronic nerve compression injury is a disease initially mediated by the Schwann cells, with
early reactive changes being Schwann cell proliferation and apoptosis independent of axonal
pathology.
Ischemia
After more than 15 minutes of anoxia, axonal transport stops.
Axonal transport can recover if reperfusion occurs within 12 to 24 hours.
Nerve Regeneration After Injury
Nerve regeneration across the zone of injury begins with axonal elongation.
Schwann cells migrate from the distal and proximal nerve stumps of a disrupted axon and
attempt to form Büngner bands (columns) to assist directed axonal growth (ie, guide the tip
or growth cone of the axon or fiber).
Neurotrophic factors influence the growth cone.

Reinnervation of muscle only occurs if the muscle has viable motor end plates that can be
stimulated by a regenerating nerve.
Soon after injury, the affected muscle increases the number of its motor end plates.
With continued fibrosis, the number of motor end plates decreases.
After 12 to 18 months, motor end plates of an affected muscle have decreased by a large
number so that meaningful reinnervation is not possible.
1 inch per month, 1 mm per day is the general guideline of how quickly a nerve can recover.
Physical Examination

Physical Examination
Physical examination of the patient by a clinician with a keen knowledge of anatomy is a
critical component in determining the extent of the peripheral nerve injury. Evaluation of
a patient’s sensory and motor function distal to the site of injury is most useful. As
shown in Figure 1, a complete motor examination helps the clinician localize the site of
the pathology along the course of the nerve, starting from the nerve root to the distal
portion of the terminal branches. A thorough and orderly physical examination also
allows for the information obtained to be more objective than subjective. This improves
communication between clinicians and improves longitudinal follow-up of the patient
and determination of the patient’s progress. A thorough, objective physical examination
is the most effective method for the evaluation of a patient in whom peripheral nerve
injury is suspected.

Muscle Strength Grading
Grade 5: full strength; contraction allows for motion through full arc of motion against full
resistance.
Grade 4:– reduced strength; contraction allows for motion through full arc of motion against
reduced resistance.

Grade 3: strength is weak; contraction allows for motion through near full arc of motion only
against gravity.
Grade 2: strength is very weak; contraction allows for motion through near full arc of motion
only if gravity is removed.
Grade 1: muscle contraction only; contraction results in no appreciable joint motion even with
gravity removed.

Muscle Strength Grading
The Medical Research Council Scale for Muscle Strength is the most frequently used
system for determining muscle strength. Slight variations in this system exist between
clinicians; however, the system used by the clinician must be well defined and remain
consistent. A “+” or a “-”after the number is common; these are examples of
modifications made by clinicians and should be used sparingly. Although adding
qualifiers to the Medical Research Council Scale score may seem helpful, doing so may
make the score more subjective than objective because the meaning of these qualifiers
seldom is well defined (eg, the difference between grade 5- and grade 4+ is not defined).
Sensation
Determine if sensation is normal or abnormal.
If abnormal, determine to what degree sensation is abnormal. Sensation testing is inherently
subjective, requiring that the clinician be as specific as possible to decrease the subjectivity of
the examination.
Specific tests
Ten testing: on a scale of 0 to 10, the patient subjectively reports how close to normal
sensation is compared with the contralateral/uninjured side; 0 = no sensation, 10 = normal
sensation.
Two-point discrimination: use a two-point disk-criminator
Static: apply pressure over specific points
Dynamic: apply pressure and drag it longitudinally along the length of the
dermatome/sensory distribution to be tested
Semmes-Weinstein monofilament: cutaneous threshold pressure test

Diagnostic Studies

Diagnostic Studies
The primary objective diagnostic studies for peripheral nerve injuries are
electromyography and nerve conduction studies. These studies assess the function of
sensory nerves, motor nerves, and the muscles to confirm neuropathies versus
myopathies. These studies are critical for determining the diagnosis and the level of
injury and for identifying any recovery from these injuries. Recently, imaging studies,
such as ultrasonography and magnetic resonance neurography, have become
increasingly used to determine not only the presence of a peripheral nerve injury but
also the degree of nerve injury.
Nerve Conduction Studies
Sensory nerve function
Stimulating a mixed (motor and sensory) nerve produces a compound nerve action potential.
Stimulating a sensory nerve produces a sensory nerve action potential.
Testing the nerve can be done by stimulating the nerve in a proximal to distal (antidromic)
manner or distal to proximal (orthodromic) manner.
Velocity of conduction is known if the distance travelled (in millimeters) and time
(milliseconds) is known.
Latency is the difference between the time of stimulation and the time of onset of action
potential.
Velocity and latency are affected by many factors.
Temperature
Age
Demyelination
Loss of axons
Amplitude of sensory nerve action potential is an important measure and is increased by
decreasing temperatures and decreased by increasing age.
Motor nerve function

Stimulating a motor nerve produces a compound muscle action potential. This is a single
motor nerve stimulating multiple muscle fibers.
Compound muscle action potential measures the velocity of the impulse over the nerve and
the transmission of that signal across the neuromuscular conduction through the muscle
fibers.
F-waves occur if a signal travels orthodromically (proximally) and depolarizes the motor
neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord, which (if the stimulation is sufficiently large)
will cause the cells of the anterior horn to discharge another antidromic signal that is
recorded in the muscle after the initial compound muscle action potential.
Electromyography
Electromyography covers an entire motor unit (anterior horn cell of the spinal cord, motor
neuron, and muscle).
Measures
Insertional activity: activity of a muscle if the needle electrode is inserted into the muscle
Decreased activity: poor muscle viability, muscle fibrosis, muscle atrophy
Increased activity: sign of denervation or primary muscle disorder (eg, myopathy)
Spontaneous activity: electrical discharges in muscle that occur without muscle contraction
and without movement of the testing needle
Fibrillations: occur in denervated muscle fibers and some myopathies 2 to 3 weeks after the
onset of injury
Graded by density (eg, 1+ to 4+) and amplitude
Higher amplitude: earlier
Lower amplitude: later
Not visible: only detectable on electromyography
Positive sharp waves: abnormal electrical discharges of single muscle fibers
Can be seen with fibrillations if muscle is denervated
If only muscle damage, then seen without fibrillations.
As seen with fibrillations, takes 2 to 3 weeks to appear.
Fasciculations: spontaneous discharges of a single motor unit
Can be detected clinically (ie, visible)
Nonspecific to various neuromuscular disorders
Motor unit action potentials:– characterized by duration, amplitude, shape, recruitment

Amplitude of an motor unit action potential characterizes the density of the muscle fibers
within the motor unit.
Duration and shape are affected by quality of conduction.
Recruitment: rate of motor unit action potential generation
Helps differentiate muscle weakness as the result of the decrease in the number of
peripheral motor neurons and motor units or the result of a central problem in recruitment
Ultrasonography
Advantages
Allows for dynamic testing (useful in patients with presumptive thoracic outlet syndrome)
Able to follow the nerve along its course to localize the site of the pathology
With a skilled ultrasonographer, has the potential to determine the internal pathology of the
nerve as is observed in patients with brachial neuritis
Noninvasive and easy for the patient
Disadvantages
Challenging and requires a skilled ultrasonographer with an appropriately high-resolution
ultrasonography machine
Limited objective correlation with disease state/condition, other than detailing the size of the
nerve
Magnetic Resonance Neurography
Advantages
Can image nerves anywhere in the body
Can be obtained at any point, dissimilar from electrodiagnostic studies in which information
in the first few weeks is not as helpful
Continually improving resolution
Disadvantages
Expensive and time-consuming to obtain (eg, may be difficult for the patient to lie still)
Dissimilar from ultrasonography, magnetic resonance neurography evaluates a specific
section of the body. It cannot easily follow/trace a nerve along its course down the arm
without necessitating additional scans (increasing cost and time in the magnetic resonance
scanner for the patient).

Spinal Cord Injury

Spinal Cord Injury
Spinal cord injury is one of the most devastating survivable effects from trauma. Spinal
cord injury not only directly affects daily function and necessitates some degree of
function dependent on others but also risks compromise to the patient’s
cardiopulmonary system, skin, coagulation and hemostasis, and metabolism. The degree
of a patient’s deficit also is highly variable, with patients presenting with a wide range of
functional deficits. This is a result of not only the density of the deficit but also the levels
of spinal cord injury. Peripheral nerve injuries are lower motor neuron injuries. Because
the spinal cord is a component of the central nervous system, spinal cord injuries are
upper motor neuron injuries. The starting point for understanding spinal cord injury is
determining the level and completeness of the injury.
American Spinal Injury Association Classification
Motor Grading
0: total paralysis
1: palpable or visible contraction
2: active movement, full range of motion if gravity is eliminated
3: active movement, full range of motion against gravity
4: active movement, full range of motion against moderate resistance
5: active movement, full range of motion against full resistance
Sensory Grading
0: absent
1: altered (decreased or impaired)
2: normal
American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale Summary

A: complete; no sensory or motor function is preserved caudal to the injury level.
B: sensory incomplete (but motor complete); sensory but not motor function is preserved
below the neurologic level of injury.
C: motor incomplete; motor function is preserved at the most caudal sacral levels or patient
meets criteria for sensory incomplete status and has some sparing of motor function more
than three levels below the motor level; fewer than 50% of key muscle functions below the
neurologic level of injury have a muscle grade.2
D: motor incomplete; same as defined earlier, except 50% of key muscle functions below the
neurologic level of injury have a muscle grade.2
E: normal; sensation and motor function are graded as normal in all segments and the patient
had prior deficits.
Mechanism of Injury
Direct physical or mechanical injury (primary)
Primary injury that occurs at time of injury
Direct impact to or mechanical disruption of neuron cell body, axonal tract, supporting cells,
and vasculature
Physiologic
Secondary damage
Complex interaction of several factors: release of inflammatory mediators and endogenous
opioids, activation of inflammatory cells, induction of oxidative free radicals, damage to
axonal myelin sheaths, increase in vascular permeability and thrombosis, production of
excitotoxic neurotransmitters, induction of cellular necrosis and apoptosis, ingress, and
differentiation of regenerative cells
This list includes multiple potential targets for therapy. Various cellular and pharmacologic
agents are under investigation for decreasing the physiologic mediators of damage in
patients with spinal cord injury.
Management
Initial evaluation: Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol
Airway, breathing, and circulation always first
Close attention to potential neurogenic shock: hypotension without tachycardia
Loss of autonomic control caused by loss of sympathetic control

Maintain mean arterial pressure greater than 85 mm Hg to prevent additional ischemia.
A thorough neurologic examination is performed next.
Key innervations of cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral
Sacral
Motor: external anal sphincter tone
Sensory: deep rectal sensation
Assessment of spinal reflex function
Determine American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale.
Presence of spinal shock
No motor, sensory, deep tendon reflexes with absence of bulbocavernosus reflex
Only after bulbocavernosus reflex has returned can the inherent function of the spinal cord
and American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale be determined.
Prevention of iatrogenic injury
Appropriate immobilization of every spine injury
Cervical: well-fitting cervical collar; in-line stabilization of the head, neck, and shoulders
should be maintained by one provider if the collar is being removed or is removed.
Thoracolumbar: flat bed without an elevated head and moving patient as infrequently as
possible
Traditional log-rolling method may place torsional forces on the spine.
Obtain appropriate imaging studies.
Definitive management: three overarching goals
Physical decompression in the zone of injury to limit irreversible primary neurologic injury
Restoration of mechanical stability to prevent secondary insult because of biomechanic
instability of the spine
Optimization of the local environment in preparation for the reparative/regenerative phase
Neurologic stabilization
Maintain mean arterial pressure greater than 85 mm Hg
High dose methylprednisolone sodium succinate infusion in acute injury window was
initially encouraging; however, follow-up studies did not show a desirable risk-benefit
ratio.
Other immune modulators (eg, interleukin-10, minocycline, NSAIDs, and atorvastatin)
have been investigated; however, follow-up studies did not reproduce initial optimistic
results.
Other factors currently are being investigated, specifically, factors that impede the
supraphysiologic activation of glutamate receptors.

Regenerative
Neural tissue damage in the central nervous system initiates physiologic and mechanical
responses that remove cellular, axonal, and myelin debris.
Reparative glial cells and neurite budding proliferation follows removal of cellular debris.
Targets for therapy include optimization of the neural regrowth and support.
Inhibiting neurite outgrowth inhibitor A
Promoting neurotrophic factors capable of inducing growth
Cellular therapy: stem cell and pluripotent cell technologies
